question: What did Lewis and Rao (2015) 'The Unfavorable Economics of Measuring the Returns to Advertising' find about the noise in measuring advertising effects and required sample sizes? Include other peer-reviewed studies on statistical power of ad experiments with specific numbers.

output.content:
### Lewis and Rao (2015)

Lewis and Rao analyzed **25 randomized digital-advertising field experiments** involving major U.S. retailers and financial firms, more than **$2.8 million in ad spending**, and generally **500,000–1,000,000+ users per experiment**. Their conclusion was not that advertising has no effect, but that causal effects are often too small relative to individual-level sales noise to estimate precisely. [[1, 2]]

- Individual sales were extremely volatile: the **standard deviation of sales was typically about 10 times the mean** over the campaign-evaluation window; retailers’ coefficient of variation generally ranged from **4 to 23**, clustering around **10–15**. [[1]]
- For retail experiments, the median standard error of estimated ROI was **26.1 percentage points**, implying a median **95% confidence interval more than 100 percentage points wide**. For financial-service experiments, the median ROI standard error was **115%**. [[1]]
- A representative example had an estimated advertising impact of only **$0.35** against a **$75** individual-level sales standard deviation—a signal-to-noise ratio of **0.0047** and an incremental \(R^2\) of approximately **0.0000054**. With **2 million users**, even a true **25% ROI** produced an expected \(t\)-statistic of only **1.04**; the experiment would fail to reject zero effect about **74% of the time**. [[1]]
- At typical digital-ad intensity, distinguishing **zero ROI from positive ROI** generally required **single-digit millions of person-weeks**; the paper’s broader summary says informative experiments could require **more than 10 million person-weeks**. [[2, 3]]
- For the 25 experiments, only **3** had sufficient power to reliably determine that a campaign was highly profitable; the median experiment would have needed to be approximately **9 times larger** for that purpose. [[1]]
- Detecting a much smaller distinction—such as **0% versus 10% ROI**—was substantially harder; related calculations indicate that **hundreds of millions of subjects** could be required. [[4]] 

The underlying problem is therefore a **signal-to-noise problem**, not simply inadequate tracking: advertising is inexpensive per person, while purchases are sparse and highly dispersed across consumers.

### Other peer-reviewed evidence

| Study | Design and sample | Power/precision finding |
|---|---:|---|
| **Johnson, Lewis & Reiley (2017), *Marketing Science*** | Randomized display-ad experiment involving approximately **3 million Yahoo users** who were prior customers of a national retailer | Estimated a **3.6% sales increase**. Adding “control ads” removed unaffected observations and improved precision by **31%**, equivalent to increasing the sample from 3.0 million to **5.3 million users**. Covariate adjustment improved precision only **5%**; combining the methods improved precision **34%**, equivalent to approximately **5.6 million users**. [[5, 4]]|
| **Johnson, Lewis & Reiley (2017), power calculations reported in the same study** | Their earlier comparable experiment had roughly **1.6 million users** | Estimated power was only **47%** for the relevant sales-effect test. In the new design, reducing the sales standard deviation from **$125 to $111** raised calculated power from **49% to 79%**, illustrating that variance reduction can be more valuable than simply adding observations. [[4]]|
| **Johnson, Lewis & Reiley (2017), “Online Display Ad Effectiveness Funnel & Carryover,” peer-reviewed field-experiment study** | **432 Google Display Network experiments**, **431 advertisers**, about **2.2 billion user observations**; average experiment size approximately **4 million users** | Based on Lewis–Rao power calculations, the median experiment required about **3.3 million exposed-user observations** merely to distinguish break-even from an ineffective campaign, and approximately **1.3 billion observations** to detect a **5% difference** in marketing outcomes. [[6]]|
| **Gordon, Zettelmeyer, Bhargava & Chapsky (2019), *Marketing Science*** | **15 Facebook experiments**, **500 million user-experiment observations** and **1.6 billion impressions**; individual studies ranged from **2 million to 140 million users** | The paper’s main result concerns causal identification rather than power: even these exceptionally large experiments did not make observational methods reliably reproduce randomized estimates. The scale illustrates that millions—or tens of millions—of users may be needed before ad-effect estimates become statistically informative. [[7, 8]]|
| **Yelp field experiment, peer-reviewed research cited in the literature** | **18,294 restaurants**, with **7,209 randomly assigned** to receive ads for three months; roughly **500 million paid-search impressions** | For an outcome subsample of **5,867 restaurants**, the minimum detectable effect was approximately **0.046 standard deviations** at 5% significance and **80% power**—a useful contrast showing that business-level randomization can yield more favorable power than noisy individual purchase outcomes. [[9]]|

### Bottom line

Lewis and Rao’s result is a warning against interpreting a large \(N\) as automatically decisive. With ad experiments, the treatment often explains an extraordinarily small share of sales variation. Consequently, even million-user experiments can have low power, while modestly improving the outcome measure or experimental design—such as control ads that remove irrelevant sales noise—can deliver the equivalent of millions of additional observations.

# When Less Is More: Data and Power in Advertising Experiments
## Abstract
Research partnered with a nationwide retailer to study the effects of online display advertising on both online and in-store purchases. We use a randomized field experiment on 3 million Yahoo! users who are also past customers of the retailer. We find statistically significant evidence that the retailer ads increase sales 3.6% relative to the control group. We show that control ads boost measurement precision by identifying and removing the half of in-campaign sales data that are unaffected by the ads.
Less data give us 31% more precision in our estimates—equivalent to increasing our sample to 5.3 million users. By contrast, we only improve precision by 5% when we include additional covariate data to reduce the residual variance in our experimental regression. The covariate-adjustment strategy disappoints despite exceptional consumer-level data including demographics, ad exposure levels, and two years’ worth of past purchase history.
## Suggested Citation
Garrett A. Johnson & Randall A. Lewis & David H. Reiley, 2017. "**When Less Is More: Data and Power in Advertising Experiments**," Marketing Science, INFORMS, vol. 36(1), pages 43-53, January.

# A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook
## Abstract
Using data from 15 U.S. advertising experiments at Facebook comprising 500 million user-experiment observations and 1.6 billion ad impressions, we contrast the experimental results to those obtained from multiple observational models. The observational methods often fail to produce the same effects as the randomized experiments, even after conditioning on extensive demographic and behavioral variables.
We also characterize the incremental explanatory power our data would require to enable observational methods to successfully measure advertising effects. Our findings suggest that commonly used observational approaches based on the data usually available in the industry often fail to accurately measure the true effect of advertising.
## Suggested Citation
Brett R. Gordon & Florian Zettelmeyer & Neha Bhargava & Dan Chapsky, 2019. "**A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook**," Marketing Science, INFORMS, vol. 38(2), pages 193-225, March.
